title: Permutation in String Problem

notes: A permutation uses exactly the same characters with the same frequencies as s1.
Only lowercase English letters occur in valid inputs.
constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: The substring "ba" is a permutation of "ab".
No substring of length 2 in s2 has the same character frequencies as s1.

content.problemStatement:
With two strings `s1` and `s2`, output `true` if `s2` includes a permutation of `s1`, or `false` otherwise.

In other words, output `true` if one of `s1`'s permutations is the substring of `s2`.

**Example 1:**

```
Input: s1 = "ab", s2 = "eidbaooo"
Output: true
Explanation: s2 contains one permutation of s1 ("ba").
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input: s1 = "ab", s2 = "eidboaoo"
Output: false
```

**Constraints:**

* `1 <= s1.length, s2.length <= 10^4`
* `s1` and `s2` consist of lowercase English letters.

hidden.label: Near match with one frequency off
Same distinct characters but mismatched frequencies
Maximum s2 length with match at final window
Maximum equal lengths with impossible frequency
Maximum equal lengths with exact permutation

notes: The advertised function signature is used by the language-specific drivers.
If s1 is longer than s2, no valid window exists.
Comparing 26 frequency entries is constant time under the lowercase-English-letter constraint.
solution.approach: Maintain a fixed-size sliding window of length s1.length in s2. Store the frequency of each lowercase letter in s1 and in the current window. When the window moves, add the incoming character and remove the outgoing character. If the two 26-element frequency arrays match, the window is a permutation of s1.
solution.timeComplexity: O(m + n), where m = s1.length and n = s2.length.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space because the alphabet has exactly 26 lowercase English letters.

bruteForce.description: Enumerate every substring of s2 having length s1.length and compare its character counts with s1. This avoids maintaining state between adjacent windows but repeats almost all work for overlapping windows.
bruteForce.complexity: O((n - m + 1) * m) time and O(1) auxiliary space when counts are maintained per window.

better.description: For each length-m window, sort the window and compare it with sorted s1. This is simpler than a frequency array conceptually, but sorting every overlapping window repeats substantial work.
better.complexity: O((n - m + 1) * m log m) time and O(m) temporary space.

optimal.description: Use a sliding window and 26-element frequency arrays. Build the required frequency array from s1, then update only the two characters affected when the window advances. A matching frequency array means the current window is a permutation of s1.
optimal.complexity: O(m + n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

hints: A valid match must have exactly s1.length characters, so consider fixed-size windows in s2.
Two strings are permutations of each other exactly when every character occurs the same number of times.
Because the input uses only 26 lowercase letters, two fixed-size frequency arrays are enough.
When the window moves one position, only the incoming and outgoing characters need their counts updated.
followUps: How would the solution change if the alphabet were Unicode instead of lowercase English letters?
Can you implement the sliding window using a single mismatch counter rather than comparing all 26 counts each time?
What changes if the input strings arrive as a stream and s2 cannot be stored entirely in memory?
learningObjectives: Recognize permutation and anagram problems as character-frequency matching problems.
Apply a fixed-size sliding-window technique to avoid recomputing overlapping windows.
Use a bounded alphabet to achieve O(1) auxiliary space.
Handle window entry and exit updates without off-by-one errors.
